assumptions.summary: The company begins with a dynamic 370-position occupation distribution and seven job types.
Friendship and information-flow ties are virtual because the paper says real data are unavailable; leadership edges are directed.
Ability grows monthly toward a position-specific ceiling and dissatisfaction rises when the next-position threshold is not met.
The annual company churn rate is fixed at 18% and AHP weights rank the five effects for monthly demission.
Three budget simulations use Poisson recruitment/demission while the position mix remains stable.
The stress case raises JM and ES churn to 30%, forbids external recruitment, and allows only qualified internal promotion.

the Summary turns a company brief into a multiplex simulation chain: State the Human Capital Network, four layers, five events, churn, budget, and sensitivity outputs before narrowing the extreme-condition result.

a management need becomes a dynamic human-capital model: Move from organizational complexity and HR practice to the manager's monitoring need, then choose a multiplex network and a dynamic occupation distribution.

bold assumptions make a flexible occupation distribution possible: List promotion, timing, churn, and priority assumptions, allocate 370 positions, and state why replacement keeps the distribution universal.
each network layer answers a different organizational relation: Define department, friendship, information-flow, and leadership edges, then bind each relation to a distinct influence index.

missing real data trigger virtual networks and interpretable indices: Acknowledge missing data, use experience-based virtual ties, and compute department, friendship, message, and leader-changing influence with explicit formulas.

ability thresholds turn promotion pressure into churn pressure: Define position, ability, growth ceiling, next-level threshold, and location, then make unmet promotion expectation raise occupation dissatisfaction.

a monthly event order converts a static graph into an automaton: Separate demission, promotion, transfer, recruitment, and settlement, and keep the first four at month start while settlement closes the month.

AHP weights turn five effects into a demission priority: Set position-specific churn, apply AHP weights to dissatisfaction and four network effects, and rank employees for the required monthly departures.

monthly plots are checked against an ideal steady-state equation: Read recruitment crests, employee troughs, and the 285-295 stable band, then compare the 18% simulation with the 291-person ideal value.

ability is passed through adverse effects to organization productivity: Sum ability scores, subtract a half-weighted demission index, and read the direct ability effect separately from indirect network effects.

budget simulations hand cost categories to a stability claim: Use three Poisson recruitment simulations, explain manager-cost dominance and IS-to-ES promotion, and read training ratios as stable before reporting the budget table.
churn sensitivity turns steady-state gaps into a staffing decision: Change churn to 18%, 25%, and 35%, compare simulated and theoretical staffing, and conclude that 80% occupancy is not sustained.

a no-recruitment stress case ends with an explicit model boundary: Raise JM/ES churn to 30%, forbid external recruitment, read the leader vacancy and 200-person decline, then pair strengths with random-edge and omitted-family limits.

results_trace.summary: At 18% churn, total personnel declines initially and then fluctuates around 285-295; the ideal steady-state calculation gives 291.
Ability rises before productivity stabilizes around 600-700 while the average demission index increases toward a steady stage.
The three budget simulations keep training-cost ratios similar and report close total budgets, with manager recruiting costs prominent.
At 25% and 35% churn, simulated staffing approaches lower theoretical steady values and cannot maintain 80% occupancy.
With 30% JM/ES churn and no external recruitment, total staff falls toward 200 and leader vacancies reach nine after two years.
The conclusion claims a comprehensive multiplex model but admits random same-layer edges and omitted subjective employee factors.

source.title: Simulation company: a dynamic model based on the Multiplex Network

source_quality.summary: All 21 pages were read and visually reviewed. The paper moves from HR complexity through a four-layer Human Capital Network, a five-event monthly automaton, churn/productivity results, budget simulation, sensitivity, and a no-recruitment stress case with explicit weaknesses.

decisions: which network relation affects a personnel, when a promotion or transfer is possible, whether steady staffing meets 80% occupancy, and how a no-recruitment policy damages leadership coverage
inputs: 370-position occupation diagram, personnel layers, virtual friendship/message ties, leadership tree, ability thresholds, churn rates, costs, and policy scenarios
outputs: monthly staff/churn series, productivity proxy, recruiting/training budget, sensitivity curves, and stress-case vacancy summary

title: Simulation company: a dynamic model based on the Multiplex Network
unresolved_questions: The Summary promises a comprehensive Human Capital Network and budget/sensitivity outputs, but those outputs remain simulation claims with no calibration dataset.
The Introduction reconstructs a nine-issue management request, but the official contest wording is not available in the source paper.
The occupation distribution allocates 370 positions through priority rules, but the source does not provide an executable diagram specification or real staffing validation.
Department influence divides vacancy by capacity minus one; denominator edge cases, vacancy definitions, and zero-capacity handling are not specified.
Friendship, PageRank, and leadership effects rely on virtual ties, unspecified PageRank settings, and a distance convention that is not fully released.
The dissatisfaction index treats ability growth and promotion threshold as sufficient churn pressure while subjective motivations are omitted.
AHP weights dominate the demission ranking, but the pairwise judgments, normalization, and sensitivity to weight changes are not shown.
Promotion and transfer algorithms are described in prose but no executable ordering, tie handling, or implementation trace is supplied.
The 18% simulation reaches a 285-295 band and a 291-person ideal value, but the result is not an uncertainty interval or independent validation.
The multiplex network is updated by adding and deleting nodes, yet the edge-refresh policy after each personnel event is not reproducibly frozen.
Productivity subtracts half the demission index from ability, a constructed proxy with no observed productivity outcome or scale calibration.
The three budget simulations use Poisson recruitment/demission and stable position types, but source costs, random seeds, and forecast error are not released.
The 25% and 35% sensitivity cases show lower theoretical staffing and higher recruitment cost, but only three churn scenarios are tested.
The no-recruitment stress case reaches about 200 employees and nine leader vacancies in two years, but the stress policy and promotion eligibility are stylized.
The strengths and weaknesses admit random within-layer edges and omitted subjective employee factors, limiting generalization beyond this simulation.
